articles.title: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres
articles.description: As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking out Sandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.” The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit. Continue reading...

articles.title: Small molecular twists may strengthen nature's magnetic compass
articles.description: A collaborative research team led by Yasuhiro Kobori at Kobe University, together with researchers from Toho University, Saitama University, Nagoya Institute of Technology and the University of Freiburg, has identified a potential molecular mechanism that could enhance magnetic compass responses in cryptochrome, a blue-light-sensitive protein implicated in magnetoreception.

articles.title: Hopkins, your public safety alerts have been inadequate.
articles.description: Under the Jeanne Clery Campus Safety Act, the University, as a participant in federal financial aid programs, is required to report campus crime and/or violence to students. These reports are not strictly limited to those that occur on campus buildings: Institutions of higher education must also include events that occur at on-campus student housing and public property within or immediately adjacent to campus bounds. Furthermore, the Clery Act requires that campus officials evaluate if there is a serious or ongoing threat regarding a crime included within the act. If the threat is serious or ongoing, a timely warning must be issued. The University's Public Safety advisories legally comply with the Clery Act in their coverage of locale and in their timely warnings. The University currently employs multiple methods of campus security alerts including Homewood Campus Security Alerts mailing list and the RAVE Emergency Alert Text Message System. Subscription to these systems are encouraged among university resources and communications, especially to new students. However, over the past two years, several instances of the University's Public Safety communication alerts have raised concern among the student body, including members of The Editorial Board. While we understand that the following examples are too little in number to broadly characterize all alerts, we still believe that it is important to catalogue specific untimely, vague notices. Alerts arrive late Recently, on Friday, Sept. 25 at 6:43 p.m., students received an email from the University's Office of Public Safety informing them that a potentially armed man had attempted to enter The Academy, an on-campus housing building. Neither Public Safety nor the advisory email confirmed whether or not the man possessed a weapon. Disturbingly, one Academy resident reported an eye-witness account of the man in the building as early as 2:40 p.m. Sidechat posts also circulated, warning students about an armed suspect, well before Public Safety circulated an official alert. The Academy incident is not an isolated case. On July 11, 2026, an affiliate reported being threatened with physical violence near the 3200 block of St. Paul Street at approximately 5:30 p.m. However, the "Assault by Threat" advisory was not sent out by Public Safety until 9:06 a.m. the next morning, more than 15 hours later. While the University may have legitimate and/or legal reasons for these delays, such as withholding confidential information involved in ongoing investigations, the absence of consistency in reporting standards undermines the efficacy of these alerts. Students should not have to question whether they are receiving timely and accurate information about possible threats to their safety. Alerts say too little Let's consider the email sent on Sunday, Oct. 4 at 8:55 p.m. where Public Safety informed the student body about an ongoing Baltimore Police Department (BPD) investigation regarding an incident occurring in the 100 block of West 39th Street. The email stated: "To keep you informed: Baltimore Police are currently investigating an incident that occurred in the 100 block of West 39th street on October 4, 2026, at about 7:20 p.m. Male and female suspects entered a store and were approached by an employee. One of the suspects produced a pocketknife. The suspects then left the store in an unknown direction. Suspects Description: Male, 60 yrs. armed with a pocketknife. Female, 30 yrs, no further description." A student reading such a description lacks any information that would help them recognize or avoid anyone that could pose a danger. This lack of clarity is reflected in additional Public Safety warnings, one which occurred on Oct. 14, 2026. "On October 14, 2026 at 9:30 AM, it was reported to Public Safety that an affiliate was inappropriately touched by an unknown male in the 2700 block of N. Calvert Street. The suspect was last seen walking South on N. Calvert Street. Suspect appeared disheveled and was heard making loud verbal outbursts prior to and after the incident. JHPD, BPD and Public Safety conducted a joint canvas of the area and the suspect has not been located at this time. Suspect description: Male, 5'-8", approximately 40 years old. Suspect was last seen wearing a black hoodie and black pants." While this email was sent relatively promptly at 11:34 a.m. the same day, it provides no indication of where the suspect might have gone following the incident, or whether the joint search by JHPD, BPD and Public Safety was making progress. Sometimes, RAVE alerts also mislead students with vague location details. On Sep. 25, 2025, the University sent out an advisory notice about the BPD investigating a Hopkins affiliate being approached and struck by an unknown object at 7:30 a.m. The advisory notice said "occurred in the area of St Paul and 34 Street," but this is better recognized as the block between McCoy and Wolman Hall. Using terminology that requires a map to decode is not helpful to students who quickly open their phone to see an alert notification. Some incidents never get an alert In Fall 2025, The News-Letter was informed by multiple sources about a female breaking into AMR II over the annual Family Weekend. In an interview with The News-Letter, a resident of AMR II at that time shared their account of watching a female being escorted off of the premises. The resident described her to be potentially intoxicated and needing medical attention and "wearing paper towels as shoes," along with carrying trash bags. The University declined to comment on this account. In addition, multiple residents in AMR II confirmed that during that time, Resident Advisors were informing the students to lock doors, citing instances of non-Hopkins affiliates entering residential buildings. Regarding this event, the University did not send any communication or alert to the student body. Even when looking into this topic, the details about this were sparse aside from a few concerns on Sidechat. This misalignment with student reports to the University's (or the lack thereof) concerns us. Student behavior may be impacted by knowledge of certain events happening on campus, served by the public safety alerts, whether it is to take a different route home late at night or be increasingly vigilant by routinely locking doors rather than propping them open. Comparing Hopkins alerts to peer institutions Several of the University's peer institutions are bound to the same commitments of the Clery Act; however, some institutions include additional information that the Hopkins Public Safety's current communications does not regularly provide that we feel to increase the comprehension and actionability of public safety alerts. We suggest to the University to take these inclusions into consideration: Massachusetts Institute of Technology MIT's reports have included any available photo or video footage of the suspect, and similarly to Hopkins, provide students with an actionable list of items for how to remain safe and work to prevent such occurrences. If MIT can provide students with photos of suspects beyond simple descriptions, then Hopkins - with more than a thousand security cameras that are part of campus safety initiatives - may be able to do so as well. University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) With many incidents reported through the UC Berkeley WarnMe Timely Warning, UC Berkeley also includes a definition of the crime that it can be categorized as. For instance, their definition for sexual battery reads "...a type of sexual assault in which a private body part of another person is touched without the consent of the survivor for the purpose of sexual gratification, including instances where the survivor is incapable of giving consent." By including definitions, the students are provided with a mental scaffold of the event that is not limited to the physical actions that occurred but also potentially allow better understanding of the emotional and long-term consequences of incidents. This also may encourage better recognition of occurred actions to be crimes in students' lives as they are reminded of what fits the definition of a crime. Stanford University Stanford's AlertSU Timely Warning system, which acts similarly to the RAVE Alerts, includes race. Hopkins' RAVE Alerts currently do not provide race. Race can be an important identifying marker when added with other details, such as clothing, height and age, which the University already provides. Conclusion The University must make a greater effort in ensuring that its public safety communications are timely, transparent and consistent in nature. Students are legally entitled to a comprehensive overview of potentially dangerous incidents, as well as actionable information and instructions that help them make informed decisions about their safety. Student safety is something that happens in real time. As one of the nation's highly-ranked universities, we understand that Hopkins has an inherent interest in maintaining a reputation as a safe institution for prospective students. However, the University's image should not come at the cost of keeping current students in the dark regarding campus violence and crime. We encourage the University to ensure that its reputation is built upon a commitment to keeping its community safe, rather than a facade that attempts to minimize the truth. We ask that Hopkins consider what they think is most worth protecting.

articles.title: Two colleges. One culture.
articles.description: Sensitive Content Warning: This article contains partial details and mentions of sexual harassment and assault. If you are a victim of sexual violence, please know you can consult confidential or non-confidential University-based resources or Sexual Assault Resource Connectors. In a report published by the Cornell Sun, seven students have allegedly drugged and gang raped a fellow Cornell student, aliased as Jane Doe, at a Chi Phi frat party in 2024. (Be cautious: the descriptions are thorough.) The story quickly went viral as a wave of survivors and activists came outpouring with support. On the institutional side, Cornell students and alumni expressed heavy criticism at the school's handling of the matter. It is bad enough that Cornell, an institution of high academic esteem - much like ours in many ways - is accused of not pursuing adequate punishment for perpetrators and providing protections for the survivor. For Hopkins students, the easy response is to react in outrage, wish the survivor healing and move on with life. However, we sustain that the culture which enabled sexual assault also exists at Hopkins - and it is our responsibility as students to fight against that. This cannot be another flash-in-the-pan viral story, like that of Brock Turner and a similar frat sexual assault at Stanford. We must transform outrage into a real cultural shift, one that condemns sexual assault of every type at Hopkins. A college culture that allows sexual assault simply cannot be allowed to exist any longer. In the previous school year, The News-Letter examined complaints about the Office of Institutional Equity's (OIE) handling of sexual misconduct. Survivors' stories reveal a perceived indifference toward their grievances - a concerning detail, since OIE has the sole power to determine and dismiss Title IX complaints. The handling of these cases may appear to prioritize protecting Hopkins' image, which could create situations where survivors don't feel believed, heard, or protected. The prevalence of sexual assault, contrasted by low reporting rates, is not only a problem on college campuses, but something confronted by people all around the country. The CDC estimates that approximately 45% of women in the US have experienced contact sexual violence. However, in 2024, the Bureau of Justice reported that only 24% of rape and sexual assault cases were reported to the police. This reality is not one that exists solely in the realm of estimates and national statistics - the number of survivors victimized at Hopkins is shocking. Per the 2025 Annual Security & Fire Safety Report published by the Johns Hopkins Police Department (JHPD) this month, there have been an average of 4 cases of rape, around 7 cases of fondling, 8 cases of domestic violence, and around 18 cases of stalking per year from 2023 to 2025 on Homewood campus. This totals to a shocking 115 Title IX reportable offenses in the past three years. Given that these are only the cases that have been reported to JHPD and that, historically, the majority of survivors do not report, these numbers are likely significantly higher. This is indicative of a campus culture built on the protection of perpetrators and the silence of survivors. We owe it to survivors, many of them our friends and loved ones, to change that culture and replace it with one of solidarity. However, some students may say that the culture doesn't need changing. Perhaps they do not flinch at our statistics when compared to other universities. For them, we would like to propose a reintroduction to a story that has not left our minds - an attempted rape that happened on our campus last fall. A repeat sex offender, Raymond Lunn, was recently convicted for assaulting a student at 7:30 PM on a Saturday evening. We vividly remember the following scenes: loud voices proclaiming that someone should be wary about being out during that hour and the jokes that followed. The perpetrator was caught. And the story was soon buried under the leaves, to be forgotten. From an institutional, interpersonal, and individual level, we observe a campus culture that ultimately facilitates sexual coercion and rape at Hopkins - the same one that allowed Jane Doe to be victimized, the same one that keeps bystanders from stepping in. We put a call out specifically to fraternity brothers. We saw alleged members on anonymous platforms like Sidechat saying that survivors should simply tell brothers if they are a "victim." We ask that all students be reminded that survivors never have an obligation to disclose the worst moments of their life, to take on shame for something that has been done to them. I, Andrew, am inspired by many brave women to say that I am not a victim, but a survivor. And many survivors know how often institutions defend their fellow "brothers" - the perpetrators - regardless of the institution, the age, or the group. If the thought of you, the reader, speaking to me about being a survivor is uncomfortable and abrasive, I ask you to think deeply on how survivors feel in those conversations. We cannot let this moment pass without change. We, as members of the university, must not neglect our commitments, to survivors, to ourselves and to the world. We call upon students to notice misogynistic tendencies and name-calling in conversation, to interrupt intentions of forsaking bodily autonomy and turning others into sexual objects. And most of all, we swear that we will not forget the bravery of Jane Doe and the many survivors that preceded her. It is only through this promise that we might see a version of Hopkins where no one suffers the reality of sexual coercion. Andrew Huynh is a sophomore from Garden Grove, CA. studying neuroscience and public health. Vishu Sundaram is a sophomore from Bristow, VA. studying neuroscience.

articles.title: Examining what happened to the pro-Palestine movement after the encampment
articles.description: On Sept. 23, 2026 the American Civil Liberties Union and Amnesty International USA released a report examining restrictions on pro-Palestinian speech at universities across the country in the past three years. The report is based on a two-year investigation of 80 campuses across the country and includes disciplinary actions, restrictions on student organizations and increased surveillance. In the report, Hopkins was listed among the ten universities that the Trump administration's Federal Task Force to Combat Antisemitism announced it would visit in 2025 to investigate allegations that universities had failed to protect Jewish students from discrimination. At Hopkins, questions about free expression and student protest have accompanied demonstrations related to the Israel-Palestine conflict. The News-Letter examined campus protests and the outcomes of those who spoke about Palestine. Campus protests Following the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the ensuing war in Gaza, students at Hopkins organized events and protests related to the conflict. Hopkins Hillel and the Jewish Student Association organized "Stand with Israel and the Jewish Community" in solidarity with Israel to mourn Israeli lives that were lost to Hamas. The JHU Dissenters (later known as the Hopkins Justice Collective) also held a "Candlelight Vigil for a Free Palestine" to mourn the Palestinian lives lost in the conflict and a walkout to demand that the University divest from weapons manufacturers and call for a ceasefire. In the following years, the Hopkins Justice Collective (HJC) continued organizing protests and other advocacy efforts. On April 29, 2024 it began the "Palestine Solidarity Encampment" to protest the University's policies toward supporting Israel. The University responded by stressing that the encampment violated campus policies and ultimately negotiated with HJC to end the encampment on May 12, 2024. In May 2025, the HJC formed a second encampment on Keyser Quad. Within an hour, Public Safety and Johns Hopkins Police Department officers dismantled the tents and dispersed protesters. The University warned that participants could face disciplinary action, including suspension or bans. Rockwell Shapiro, a current senior at Hopkins, was suspended from May 2025 to January 2026 following his participation in the protests. During his interim suspension, Shapiro said he was unable to attend classes normally and was uncertain if he should remain in Baltimore or at Hopkins in an interview with The News-Letter. The period since May 2025 has seen fewer pro-Palestine protests than the 2023-24 academic year. Shapiro commented on how he believes the disciplinary actions that the University has taken have affected students' willingness to publicly protest. "I think other students see this and they think, 'I'm not going to protest because the cost is too high.' There were a lot of other students [who also faced disciplinary action]… I was not the only person to be put through these things. It has a chilling effect on campus," Shapiro shared. The University has also implemented or clarified policies about protests. For instance, student-led events, including protests, must receive approval from the Office of Leadership Engagement and Experiential Development (LEED). The University's current Open Space Policy also restricts face coverings on campus, except for religious or health reasons. If asked, individuals must remove masks and present identification. When asked about how he viewed the University's response to pro-Palestine protests, Shapiro discussed what he believes are connections between University leadership, financial interests and the University's approach to pro-Palestine protests. "Many of the individuals in the leadership of the University are firm in their support for Israel, and it reflects in how they manage their leadership, as well as the fact that they believe that continuing to suppress pro-Palestine movements secures financial support for the University," Shapiro alleged. In an email to The News-Letter, a University spokesperson emphasized that its approach to disciplinary action regarding student speech is focused on issues of conduct. "Statements made during public events or demonstrations, shared on public forums such as social media, or reported through complaints to university personnel or appropriate investigative units may be reviewed in consultation with the Office of Institutional Equity (OIE) and other relevant university offices to determine whether the conduct at issue may violate university policies," the spokesperson wrote. "Any such review is based on the specific circumstances and conduct at issue, not the viewpoint being expressed." SJP application process Advocacy for Palestine began at Hopkins long before the 2023 conflict. The Hopkins chapter of Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP) was founded in 2013 to raise awareness about Palestine. In the following years, SJP hosted teach-ins, film viewings, a "die-in" in 2014 and a sit-in at Garland Hall in 2019. In December 2019, the SGA deactivated SJP and several other student organizations for failing to meet audit requirements, such as a 10-member minimum. Later, in September 2024, a group of students submitted an application to reestablish SJP at Hopkins. One of the students involved in the SJP club application process, choosing to comment under the pseudonym "Blake," explained that the University initially told the group it would receive a decision by Dec. 6, 2024 in an interview with The News-Letter. Instead, the students were asked to meet with University officials on Dec. 12 to discuss the application. According to Blake, University officials initially raised concerns about the group's lack of an affiliation agreement with the national organization Students for Justice in Palestine. The students proposed changing the name to Students at Hopkins for Justice in Palestine, but they were told the University would consult the Office of the General Counsel about the name change. The group followed up with the University multiple times throughout the following months. Eventually, on Oct. 20, 2025 the University denied the application, citing the organization's name and concerns about the proposed student leader's involvement in another unrecognized organization. In an email sent to Blake, LEED wrote, "The alternative name you have selected, Students at Hopkins for Justice in Palestine, is not different or distinct enough from Students for Justice in Palestine for a reasonable individual to discern a difference between the two groups." The students attempted to appeal the decision but were told by LEED that it could not be appealed. In January 2026, they filed a complaint with the Middle States Commission on Higher Education, the accrediting organization for Hopkins. On March 27, 2026 the commission said the issue had been resolved. The University's current policies include a formal appeals process for student organization registration decisions on the basis of procedural error or new substantive information. There are also clearer guidelines regarding who can and cannot start an organization. In an interview with The News-Letter, Blake explained that the experience led them to believe that the University opposed the formation of an SJP chapter. "Hopkins doesn't want an SJP, which is clear discrimination against pro-Palestine viewpoints on campus… If it was about the viewpoint diversity, they should have no problem with an SJP forming," Blake said. Blake also expressed concern that the application process could make it difficult for student organizations to know whether they were complying with University requirements. "Part of what I worry about now is they're making it so impossible to follow their guidelines… They can use that to arbitrarily enforce their rules to make sure that certain student organizations never get approved or never have an opportunity to organize anything," Blake said. In an email to The News-Letter, a University spokesperson wrote that the University does not publicly disclose organizations that have been denied recognition. Concerns at the School of Medicine Questions about pro-Palestine organizing have also arisen at the School of Medicine. Crystal Favorito, a third-year student at the School of Medicine, is involved in starting a chapter of Medical Students for Justice in Palestine (MSJP), but MSJP's attempt in fall of 2025 to register as a student organization was unsuccessful. According to emails shared with The News-Letter by Favorito, the University placed the application on hold after identifying a social media connection between MSJP and the SJP chapter at the School of Public Health, which was under investigation by the Office of Institutional Equity. In an interview with The News-Letter, Favorito described her reaction to this decision. "The rationale that they gave was that [SJP at the School of Public Health] is under investigation, so we cannot form as a group because we've been tied to them… How does that make sense? If they can operate, then why can't we operate? I don't think we got a good rationale. The answer was just no… It was really bizarre," Favorito said. In an email to The News-Letter, a University spokesperson said the University may review prospective student organizations' affiliations with external groups. "The University reserves the right to review information (websites, social media, etc.) related to the external organization and will make the determination of whether the student organization is approved as a registered student organization (RSO). RSOs may not have affiliations with external organizations that promote behavior that violates university policy," the spokesperson wrote. MSJP has since reapplied and is currently awaiting review by the University's compliance office. Additionally, Favorito also described difficulties obtaining approval for research related to Palestine. In September 2025, she, along with other medical students, submitted a proposed survey to examine how exposure to the war in Gaza affected medical students' mental well-being and experiences of moral injury. Favorito shared some of the study's proposed questions with The News-Letter that were about students' emotional responses to the conflict. Students would be asked to rate how true each of the following statements was for them: "I am bothered by what I saw." "I feel helpless." "I feel betrayed by leaders or institutions." In December, the University declined to approve the study, citing concerns about the study's relevance and whether it approached the issue neutrally in an email to Favorito and the other students involved with the study. "I don't see any clear nexus to the University. In this regard, in my experience we have not approved a research survey of our own affiliates that considers broad political issues or international affairs," the University wrote to Favorito. "Why does the survey take a pro-Palestinian perspective instead of a neutral perspective? The survey itself as framed could inadvertently produce MID [moral injury and distress] in participants." In an email to The News-Letter, a University spokesperson explained the criteria considered during the review process. "During this process, we consider such questions as the nexus between the research questions and the university, why the study must focus on a university population and whether it's the right population, how participants will be recruited, and if the research team has planned to coordinate with relevant university offices (if appropriate)," they wrote. In response to questions about its handling of pro-Palestinian speech on campus, a University spokesperson said that Hopkins remains dedicated to protecting free speech. "The university's commitment to protecting free expression has not changed. We have continued to strengthen and clarify our policies and procedures and share resources intended to ensure that all members of our community can participate fully in university life in an environment free from discrimination and harassment," the spokesperson wrote.

articles.title: Graduate researchers raise concerns over reductions to University Supply Stores
articles.description: Graduate researchers, under the Teachers and Researchers United (TRU-UE) Union at Hopkins expressed concerns about operational reductions to Supply Stores writing to The News-Letter that changes would increase laboratory expenses, delay access to essential research materials and shift shipping and receiving burdens onto busy departmental staff. The Supply Stores have provided researchers on the Homewood and East Baltimore campuses with routine laboratory materials including gloves, labeling tape and reagents like cellular media. The stores supported University labs by purchasing materials at institutional prices without placing individual orders. This promoted efficiency by easily distributing commonly used materials to the labs that require them. In an email to The News-Letter, a University spokesperson stated that the reduction was due to changes in purchasing patterns and would preserve access to items requiring specialized handling or regulatory support. The new operating model took effect on October 1 and applies exclusively to the JHU Procurement-managed Supply Stores in Mudd Hall and the Pre-Clinical Teaching Building, not other University supply channels or local stockrooms. According to graduate researchers who agreed to speak with The News-Letter, a petition calling attention to the changes and demanding more University transparency has received more than 200 signatures from faculty, staff and students. Researchers said they had shared the petition with University administrators, but they had not had a formal meeting with them yet at the time of their responses. A University spokesperson confirmed they responded to the petition on Oct. 16 from the doctoral students and research community, rather than TRU-UE, after the new operating model took effect. "Communications with divisions about the changes began in early August," the spokesperson wrote. "The University is working with the union through our established processes to address any concerns that are work related." Joanna, a sixth-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Chemistry, discussed the stores' role in helping researchers keep their experiments rolling. "The Supply Stores act as intermediaries between vendors and researchers," Joanna wrote. "They purchase supplies in bulk, negotiate institutional discounts, and handle receiving, transportation, and storage of these materials." Marie, a sixth-year Ph.D. student in the Program in Molecular Biophysics in the Department of Biology, said the University announced in August that the stores would begin reducing inventory on Oct. 1. The remaining inventory would consist of a limited number of institutionally required products, such as ethanol, biohazard bags and materials requiring specialized handling or regulatory compliance. Although the stores were expected to maintain their inventory through Sept. 30, Marie reported that many workers had observed supplies beginning to dwindle throughout September. The changes affect more than access to everyday materials. Sneha, a sixth-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology's Program in Cell, Molecular, Developmental Biology and Biophysics, explained that some Supply Stores also managed shipping and receiving. In Biology, refrigerators and freezers held temperature-sensitive reagents until researchers could retrieve them. Sneha wrote that departmental administrative staff must assume additional receiving responsibilities without equivalent storage infrastructure. "Administrative offices do not have the same capacity for storage and handling of sensitive reagents that the Supply Stores did, resulting in potential degradation of expensive materials," Sneha wrote. In the Department of Chemistry, a stockroom offers some alternatives, but researchers said its capabilities cannot replace the centralized store. Joanna explained that the department is working to stock additional materials previously available through the Homewood Supply Store, but she estimated that would only cover about 75% of the supplies her laboratory needs. "Labs will now have to order those supplies directly from the vendors which not only results in longer lead times, but also greatly increases cost and the burden on our budget specialist and stockroom workers," Joanna wrote. Kelly Chen, a second-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Chemistry, said reliance on the stores extended across much of the department. "Within the Chemistry Department, almost every lab regularly purchased solvents, sample containers, protective equipment, and other items we need to carry out our work safely and successfully," Chen wrote. Chen added that undergraduate laboratory courses also obtained necessary equipment from the Supply Stores, extending the impact of the supply store reduction beyond graduate research. Marie mentioned that labs are exploring options like the University's Core Store and direct orders through suppliers like ThermoFisher, Millipore and Genesee Scientific. She mentioned that many researchers believe that the extra costs for the basic supplies that previously could be obtained through the Supply Stores will range in the thousands of dollars on a monthly basis. The researchers expressed their dissatisfaction not only with the costs involved but also with the manner in which the decision was announced. For example, Sneha said that the researchers did not have a say in the decision and raised issues about the timeline of the closure. "The decision to close Supply Stores was announced suddenly and with no input from researchers," Senha wrote. "It is unclear how this decision was reached and why the timeline was so accelerated." The University spokesperson offered a different perspective on pricing and availability of research materials, saying the transition allows researchers to compare suppliers and access a wider range of products. Marie was informed by the University's administrators that they intended to act on the petition shortly. Joanna wrote that there are avenues for collaboration between administrators and researchers to find solutions that address both research needs and operational limitations. "If the University made more of an effort to communicate to their community, I truly believe that the administration would find that people are more than willing to work with them to find constructive solutions," Joanna wrote.

articles.title: Our picks of art for Halloween 2026
articles.description: Happy Halloween! The Arts & Entertainment section presents our picks of creepy, scary or unsettling pieces of art for the spooky season! Estelle Chen: The Turn of the Screw by Henry James "I remember the whole beginning as a succession of flights and drops, a little seesaw of the right throbs and the wrong," writes the governess in the beginning of her ghost-story manuscript. Thus begins Henry James' gothic horror novella, The Turn of the Screw. A young governess is employed by an absent "Master" to look after his two children in the mansion of Bly, and everything quickly begins to splinter, seesaw, fly and drop as the governess sees the ghosts of the previous governess and another employee haunting the mansion. Do the children see them too? They grow scared - of the ghosts or of the governess? Famously ambiguous, The Turn of the Screw never commits to the truth of its supernatural elements, instead threading the line between the reality of ghosts and the mania of its main character. Ending abruptly with a shock, the novella has lent itself to famous psychoanalytic and structuralist readings - its openness to interpretation continues to haunt readers and interpreters today. Lucinda Costello-Kumfer: The X-Files created by Chris Carter Are you looking for a television show fit or the Halloween season? It's an older one, but The X-Files, created by Chris Carter, still holds up as a great show for the fall months. It follows two FBI agents, Fox Mulder (David Duchovny) and Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson), who work in a unique division of the Bureau pursuing answers to unexplained phenomena. The show has an overarching plot centering around the existence of extraterrestrial life ,and dozens of one-off episodes that investigate every kind of supernatural entity you could think of, from vampires to ghosts to a man who eats kidneys and can squeeze himself into the smallest of spaces. These plot lines, combined with the dark atmosphere of the show, make it a fantastic spooky watch. Not to mention, the two main characters are incredibly complex; both independently and in their dynamic with one another, which makes the entire experience even better. Saffron Hallett: Alien (1979) directed by Ridley Scott While the sequels, prequels and questionable Predator crossovers are more action than horror, the film that started it all was a true science-fiction monster movie: Alien. The plot follows the crew of the Nostromo as they investigate a distress signal on an exomoon. They encounter the facehuggers, spiderlike creatures who impregnate their hosts by forcing an egg down their throat, using humans as incubators for their children to burst out. As the creature grows into the Xenomorph, the members of the crew are killed one by one until only Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) and her cat remain. Using her wits, she successfully blasts it into space. The skin-crawling tension, visceral gore, and warnings regarding AI make this a truly scary film. As film critic Roger Ebert once said, it is "an intergalactic haunted house thriller." It is a most fitting compliment. River Phan: Videodrome (1983) directed by David Cronenberg What's scarier than the screens all around us? David Cronenberg's Videodrome is a prophetic science-fiction body horror from the 1980s that remains eerily representative of today's overstimulated but bleak times in the era of the ubiquitous screen. TV channel president Max Renn (James Woods) stumbles on a plotless show called "Videodrome" that only broadcasts torture and murder. Desperate to attract new viewers, Max intensely investigates the program before he realizes he has uncovered something he was never meant to see. Max's reality is already half video hallucination, but he's unprepared for the unfathomable horrors that the television will unleash. While Videodrome certainly serves as a warning for television's evils, it also offers an apocalyptic, cerebral and seedy manifesto for the video technology addict in us all. Harrison Pope: The Passage by Justin Cronin A hybrid of rip-roaring supernatural thriller and literary epic, Justin Cronin's The Passage was an instant success upon its release in 2010 - and it's not difficult to see why. Cronin combines apocalyptic horror, epic journeys and Steinbeckian interpersonal drama in a unique and compelling novel. Cronin's novel begins in a harrowing vision of an alternate America whose government hopes to harness a deadly virus in order to create the ultimate bioweapon: unstoppable vampire-like monsters. Amy, a young girl of mysterious origins, flees agents of this government seeking to use her as their latest test subject, aided only by FBI defector Brad Wolgast. After the creatures turn on their creators, the novel jumps forward a century into an apocalyptic future in which Amy and her allies fight for humanity's survival. The Passage may seem a hefty read, but its over 700 pages will fly by. Though his subject matter is bleak, Cronin weaves in an undercurrent of pathos and hope that will keep you invested. And, if you can't get enough of the original book, he's penned two sequels to sink your teeth into (pun intended). Who knew the end of the world could be so addictive? Tessa Recart: Obsession (2026) directed by Curry Barker Obsession depicts Bear Bailey (Michael Johnston), a deeply insecure man, who uses a supernatural One Wish Willow to ask his co-worker, Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrete), to love him more than anyone in the world. This is the catalyst for all the horrific and bizarre events that follow when Nikki becomes terrifyingly obsessed with Bear. Bear's desire for affection and his inability to act on it are quite relatable. This is portrayed well by Johnston, but Navarrete's acting steals the show. The scenes where her character breaks out of her trance are especially evocative: a lot of screaming, a lot of fear and a lot of pain. So, was it Bear's love that drove this story? Or was it just assault, rooted in a society that so often mistakes male desire for a call to action, no matter the cost? Watch, or maybe rewatch, this movie and draw your own conclusions. And perhaps, this spooky season, think not only about the monsters in film but also about the ones in our daily lives, who so often leave violent marks on the lives of innocent women with their obsessions. Selven Ren: Vertigo (1958) directed by Alfred Hitchcock What would you do if someone told you she had died hundreds of years ago? What if you happened to fall in love with her? What if the very woman whose death you were certain you had witnessed suddenly showed up in your life again? Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, also known as the "Master of Suspense," Vertigo is one of the most influential psychological thrillers in cinematic history. In 2012, it was named the greatest film of all time. Beyond its critical acclaim, Vertigo also gave birth to the iconic dolly zoom, commonly referred to as the "Vertigo effect." The film follows Scottie Ferguson (James Stewart), a former detective whose fear of heights has forced him into retirement. Hired to follow a mysterious woman Madeleine Elster (Kim Novak), Scottie soon finds himself entangled in a labyrinth of love, obsession and deception. The spectral score, composed by the legendary Barnard Hermann, drifts like a tender lullaby, wandering, circling and repeating, luring the audience into the maw of mystery. For all this time Scottie believed he was chasing the truth, never knowing that all he pursued was a phantom born of his own mind. Aditya Sankar: Bluebeard's Castle by Béla Bartók This spooky season, I entreat you to indulge in a haunting and barely hour-long reinterpretation of a classic folktale. Canonized by Charles Perrault, the Bluebeard story is that of a wife who uncovers the darkest secrets of her mysterious husband. Centuries later, two Bélas - Balázs, who provided the libretto, and renowned composer Bartók - united for a stunning operatic adaptation. There are four voices: the bass of Bluebeard, the soprano of his latest wife Judith, a Bard who provides a prologue, and the castle itself - a deliciously gothic landscape with a dark hall and seven closed doors. No longer is Judith a naive Eve; her quest for knowledge pushes past Bluebeard's implorement to uncover dire doors after ominous doors - each filled with fascinating imagery (and ridiculously obvious red flags). It is in the nature of an operatic tragedy that we and Judith continue to our doom, propelled by Bartók's orchestral motifs and even more unsettling pauses. Artists have returned to this opera countless times, from Michael Powell's deliriously colorful film to Pina Bausch's daring ballet. Who hasn't felt the excitement and fear of getting to know someone?

articles.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
articles.description: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

articles.title: My experience as a male survivor
articles.description: I know my experience as a male survivor will never be heard, and it's a truth I am still struggling to accept. Tapping into social media and seeing woman after woman gaining the courage to discuss their own stories while simultaneously knowing my story, no matter how eloquently written, will be shoved to the corner because "this isn't about me" and "now's not the time to bring it up" has only made me feel more and more isolated. Yes, this was an act of brutality committed against a woman. But as we are trying to reset our mindsets on acts of assault and violence, it's not women that need to cover up or act a certain way -it's men that need to be educated. Although I understand the sentiment of the statement above (and thoroughly agree with it), the language is incredibly gendered, and it leaves no room for men who were the victims to acts of assault and violence and no accountability for women who are the perpetrators in such an act. I am a man that was groomed and sexually assaulted by a woman when I was 16, and whenever I gather the courage to share that story, it's met with laughter from other men calling me a "sissy" for being upset, or wishing that they were in my place because I was "lucky." I learned to stop talking about my assault after that. However, with the stories of Jane Doe(s) being shared, I want to bring another perspective into view, one that I know so many men won't have the courage to share. I was raped less than a year ago, and I went to class the next morning. I knew the rapist, and while the first time was consensual, he used what leverage he had to coerce me into sexual acts, and when I needed comfort in a state of mental disarray and instability, he raped me. I didn't realize I was being raped until he finished. It was over before it started. I am not sure if I was drugged, asleep or simply blocked it out of my memory, but there isn't a "best" option out of the three, so it doesn't matter. All I remember was taking an Uber home, texting my closest friends, scrubbing my skin raw and falling asleep in a puddle of vomit on the bathroom floor. But the next morning, I got up and went to my 10:30 a.m. class, trying to ignore my teacher's comments about "not being myself" and empathetically asking if I wasn't feeling well. I tried to plaster a fake smile, but I never had the energy to maintain it. I was only able to take off my extracurricular duties because the other person in charge with me was one of my friends I texted the night before. Our groupchat became a bit tense after that. When I first sent the message, I'm not sure if my friends comprehended what I had sent - I don't blame them for that, as it's not everyday someone texts that in a groupchat. They had a premonition that this guy wasn't good, but the power trips, physical and psychological abuse, coercion and demands, they were aware of none of that. There's still a lot I never shared with them, and frankly, it's because I'm ashamed of myself. This past spring semester was spent in a constant array of self-harming, starving myself and sleeping at others' places because no one trusted me to live by myself. I had so many wonderful things in store that semester, and while they happened, I didn't get to enjoy any of them because of the constant looming threat that he would come back or that he would carry through with those threats. I won't sit here from behind the screen and pretend I didn't contemplate suicide; however, I didn't have the energy to create a plan, so I became passively suicidal, which was only another reason why I needed to couch hop from place to place. Yet, somehow, that was my best semester: I made Dean's List, won several awards and did a plethora of other things, so anyone who wasn't in that groupchat had no idea the amount of suffering I was in. I considered going through the legal process of reporting it, but I knew what was at stake - this was someone who was here on a student visa, and legal action would likely result in deportation. It was something I could never bring my conscience to do. I have yet to tell my mother this happened, and honestly, I don't think I ever will. I make her worry about me too much already, and I'm afraid I'll break her heart if I tell her. I can't do that to her. So, as we navigate through this awful time and listen to all the Jane Does, I want to think of all the John Does, who still believe their stories don't believe to be heard. The case at Cornell was one of many, but in bringing it to light, many more stories have been (and will be) shared. We are more than a statistic; we are human beings who were defiled, degraded and swept under the rug. To any of my Jane and John Does reading this, you deserved better. You deserve nothing less than to be heard without judgment or question of what you were wearing or how much you drank. And to my fellow John Does, you are not alone; it's rough for us because there never is a "right time" or "our time" to share our story. I want to be explicitly clear: I would never bring the story of male victims of rape and sexual assault to silence or dismantle the voice(s) of female victims, nor would this ever be an attempt to create pity for those seven men (and the hundreds more that have committed acts of brutality). Please never think such of this article. This is just the story of a John Doe at Hopkins who did what he had to do to survive an atrocity. The News-Letter allows parties to withhold the names of parties involved in alleged gender- and sexual-based violence.

articles.title: Athlete Spotlight: Aubrey Kilgore
articles.description: Senior Aubrey Kilgore is a goalkeeper and captain for the Hopkins Field Hockey team, majoring in Neuroscience and minoring in Entrepreneurship & Management. In an interview with The News-Letter, Kilgore discussed her experiences with the sport in addition to her academic commitments. Kilgore grew up near Philadelphia, the birthplace of the United States Field Hockey Association, leading her to become familiar with field hockey at a young age. She began playing field hockey when she was seven years old, starting off in a community recreational league. In fourth grade, Kilgore decided to commit to the position of the goalie, sticking through it as she joined a club field hockey team in fifth grade. "It was kind of just by chance. [The coaches] would rotate through who was going to be the goalie every single game and I just thought it would be fun to wear all the gear, [as] the goalie has a lot of foam padding on. It's a lot of extra equipment, but I really enjoyed stopping the shots. Once I got a little bit more training, I just thought that it was the best way that I could contribute to a team," she said. Kilgore continued playing throughout high school and decided to pursue a collegiate career. "I reached out to a bunch of Division III schools and Hopkins ended up being the best fit for me, and [I'm] so happy that I chose [Hopkins]. I love it here," she said. Over time and across different teams, one thing which has stayed constant throughout it all has been to have fun when playing the sport. Simultaneously, Kilgore's understanding of the sport has changed and strengthened in regards to both the technical and mental aspects of the sport, such as picking up different skills and approaching the game in a more strategic manner. She credits her coaches in high school and college for guiding her to have a positive mindset when playing and to trust her teammates. Kilgore mentions employing the mindset of "Be[ing] a goldfish," originally from the TV series Ted Lasso, in which the titular character encourages his players to let go of any mistakes that have occurred, akin to adapting the 10-second memory of the animal. "If something happens, [like] a goal goes in, or I don't make the save I want the way I wanted to make it, I'm like, 'Okay, like what's next and how can I step up in this moment?' I think that has been a huge thing. Just taking it second by second, and it doesn't matter what happened the second before... because once you start kind of ruminating [on] past things that happened, you just kind of get down on yourself," she explained. She also focuses on maintaining a positive mindset, which helps her to build stronger connections with her teammates, a responsibility of being a captain of the team. "I'm there to learn and try new things. If it doesn't work, it doesn't work. If it does work, then it's something that I can add and have in my toolkit. These two things have been huge for me: just focusing on what's right in front of you and what's next, and then also just keeping a positive attitude. Field hockey is so dependent on the team as a whole. Finding ways that I can uplift my teammates to be at their best as well has been really important for me and my mindset. I can't be a leader for everyone else if I don't have the mindset I'm telling them to have, so I think that's been a way for me to work on my own mental approach to the game," she said. When asked about her favorite shot to save, Kilgore chose the penalty stroke where a single attacker attempts to score against the goalkeeper, similar to a penalty kick in soccer. When asked about her favorite game, she chose the opportunity to play at the 2025 NCAA Division III Field Hockey Championship. While Hopkins emerged as the runner-up, Kilgore labeled the event as an important moment of her collegiate career. "[The game was] just such an insane experience. Even though the result of the game didn't go our way, the feeling of being on the field and knowing that this is the last game of your season, no matter what, and just putting it all out there on the field, was really influential to my mindset and me as a person. It doesn't compare to anything else," she said. Like most athletes, Kilgore has multiple pre-game routines, characterizing herself as "a little superstitious." She always has one of her teammates braid her two Dutch braids, drinks an Alani Nu and listens to "Dreams and Nightmares" by Meek Mill, the last one a tradition that's started since high school. Outside of field hockey, Kilgore is interested in studying cognitive aging and neurodegenerative diseases, citing that as one of her reasons for attending Hopkins. She is currently pursuing research in cognitive aging at the Gallagher Lab, conducting testing on rats in addition to data analysis tasks. "I feel like [my lab work has] given me a broad perspective on the research world as a whole, and like what I could possibly be doing," she said. Kilgore's future plans include obtaining a master's degree in Neuroscience, conducting a thesis project with her lab and pursuing a PhD, potentially in clinical research. She mentioned her previous internship at Merck as an influential experience in determining her future academic commitments. "In [Merck's] clinical trial division, I really enjoyed getting to see what sort of drugs they were working on and what the developmental pipeline looked like. That was really interesting to me," she said. To follow the precedent established by previous spotlights, The News-Letter asked her about what she wants to do or complete before graduating. "I think I really want to explore more Baltimore restaurants. I feel like I've gotten a little taste of what Baltimore has to offer, but I really just want to explore the city and [continue to] see what it has to offer," Kilgore responded. Keep an eye out for Kilgore and the rest of the field hockey team as they face Muhlenberg in Allentown, Pennsylvania this Saturday!

articles.title: Recovery without a scar: How a study on jellyfish eyes could revolutionize modern retinal care
articles.description: An estimated 1 in 1,380 people worldwide suffer from inherited or genetic retinal eye diseases, according to a 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) study. Traditional methods for managing conditions like wet macular degeneration or diabetic retinopathy are limited by human biology; once the eye is damaged, inner skin or retinal cells scar and can't be recovered. But what if a distant evolutionary ancestor could change all of that? Found several branches out from humans on the evolutionary tree, jellyfish can regenerate light-sensing organs. Their ocular structures are remarkably similar to humans, with lenses, corneas, and retinas. When a jellyfish has a damaged eye, cells zero in on regeneration rather than forming scar tissue, growing a fully functional eye and preventing further damage. Evolutionary biologist Aide Macias-Muñoz and her research team at the University of California, Santa Cruz want to study this phenomenon. The recipient of a recent $2 million NIH grant, she and her team aim to learn how jellyfish eyes regrow and whether single-cell sequencing of their DNA can help us understand future human vision gene therapy, described in an interview with The News-Letter. From her lab in Santa Cruz, Macias-Muñoz explained her plans to study two classes of Cnidaria jellyfish: box jellyfish (Tripedalia cystophora) and moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) and observe them at different life stages. This will help test her hypothesis that development and regeneration are very different. If her team can discover the neural signals that tell jellyfish eyes to regenerate instead of scar, scientists may be able to utilize that data for human eyes too. "Humans have two eyes that focus light into some cells, and then it all gets processed in a central brain... That's how [jellyfish vision] is very different. It's not centralized; it's more decentralized," Macias-Muñoz described. To understand how these complex marine invertebrates navigate the ocean without a centralized brain, her focus will be on their nerve structures. Box jellyfish have 24 eyes encircling their body like a crown, attached to four tiny sensory centers called rhopalia. These rhopalia are like mini brains hanging from their cube-shaped body; each holds six eyes to interpret images. Moon jellyfish have eight rhopalia, with two eyes each that can sense light but aren't image-forming. To study them at their earliest state, Macias-Muñoz plans to cut off the rhopalia and have the jellyfish regrow them. "We are cutting off the whole sensory structure where they have both the neurons and the eyes located," she explained. She and her research group are preparing to find potential candidates for the study and want to learn how both species recreate these biological cells anew. "Are there any cells that appeared in regeneration that were not present in development?... Is it purely stem cells that are changing when regeneration happens?... Or could there be some de-differentiation?" she asked. For human eyes, the roadblock to regeneration is our own biology. When the inner eye is damaged, scar tissue often forms and can build up, tugging at the retinal layers, creating vision issues or even pulling the retina away entirely. When this kind of damage is present, support cells called Müller glia rush in to save neurons, rapidly multiplying in a process called reactive gliosis. This process is the nervous system's defense response to seal off damaged tissue, but the scar that appears afterwards prevents new neural connections from forming. Current treatments for blinding retinal conditions like retinal vein occlusion or uveitis focus on maintaining the retina and preserving the cells that remain. Standard practice involves frequent intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF medications - specialized medications injected directly into the vitreous, the gel inside the eye, blocking the growth of abnormal blood vessels and preventing further swelling. While these injections currently hold the line for treatment, the reality of their application is much more daunting, with patients needing injections every four to six weeks. For Nelan Hughes, a senior retinal scribe in South Carolina, providing care and reassurance to these patients is an everyday task. She described sitting in the rooms with her patients and crying along with them as they slowly lose their vision. "The biggest challenge [in retinal therapy] right now is figuring out how to get the eyes to produce the medicine we're injecting into them on their own," Hughes emphasized. Clinical innovation is already attempting to fix this problem. An emerging gene therapy called RGX-314 from REGENXBIO works by introducing a virus into the eye that doesn't create a viral illness but instead delivers genetic instructions. Replacing frequent injections, this medication reprograms the eye to produce the anti-VEGF antibodies on its own. Early results are encouraging, with 78% of patients in one high-dose test group going long periods without needing additional injections. RGX-314 is currently administered during surgery, but trials are underway to incorporate it as a simple in-office procedure. While medications like RGX-314 offer hope, they work by modifying cells left behind after damage has already occurred. They still cannot rebuild what has been destroyed. "Nerve tissue doesn't regenerate," Hughes stresses. But jellyfish can override this genetic code and create something new. This is where a study like Macias-Muñoz's could revolutionize these treatment plans, offering cellular regeneration instead of continuous injections into the eye. Macias-Muñoz explained how previous gene studies produced limited results. "This has led to a "blind spot" in our understanding of whether the genetic mechanisms that dictate the ability to regenerate are fixed, or whether regeneration can happen in a number of ways," Macias-Muñoz said in a press release from UC Santa Cruz. Identifying that genetic roadblock could be the missing link the human eye needs. For patients facing a lifetime of retinal injections, that kind of transformative therapy could mean the difference between holding off blindness and empowering the eye to heal itself.
